title: The learned man of Benares
hook: tradition says a Benares pandit tested Nanak with learning and heard him sing the Oankar

segments.voice: Yesterday, cooking at the eclipse, and your line, kindly, question it. Which habit did you ask, gently, what it's for? Day seven hundred thirty-six.

A child at a kitchen table, tracing the alphabet with a fat pencil. A says apple. B says ball. Every letter is a door to one small thing. Somewhere along the way, the letters stop being seen at all. They become the furniture of reading. Today's sakhi takes us to Benares, a city of scholars on the river Ganges, where a learned man meets a traveler and they end up talking about letters, of all things. Not apple and ball. Something much bigger. Today: the learned man of Benares.
screen: `A IS FOR APPLE.` → `LETTERS BECOME FURNITURE.` → `A CITY OF SCHOLARS.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana arrive in Benares and sit by the river. A pandit, a learned man of the city, notices this traveler with no sacred marks, no scholar's books, and a musician at his side. Some tellings give him a name, Chatur Das. He comes to test the Guru. What do you know? What have you studied? What can you recite? Tradition says Nanak answered by singing. And the hymn he sang, tradition says, was the Oankar, a long composition now in the Guru Granth Sahib. Here's the clever thing about it. A pandit taught with letters: students wrote them on a wooden slate, one by one. The Oankar takes the pandit's own tools and turns them. Its verses move through the letters, and each letter becomes a door to the One. It opens with Oankar itself, the One, from whom even Brahma, the creator god of the pandit's own books, came into being. And then letter by letter, it speaks of God, of the mind, of the false and the true, of what learning is for. So the Guru doesn't throw learning away. He takes the alphabet a scholar loves and shows him where every letter points. In the tellings, the pandit listens, and bows. Notice who bows. Not a fool, but a learned man. And not because he lost an argument. Because he heard his own learning sung back to him, deeper than he'd been reading it. Sikh tradition honors study; the Gurus wrote, collected and taught. Learning bows, in this story, when it remembers what it's about.
screen: `A PANDIT TESTS THE TRAVELER.` · `THE GURU SINGS THE OANKAR.` · `EACH LETTER A DOOR TO THE ONE.` · `THE LEARNED MAN BOWS.` · then, large: `LEARNING BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one letter's meaning. Pick a letter. Any letter, in any alphabet you know. Settle and breathe. Say its sound quietly. Then let it lead you to one word that matters to you: a name, a place, a quality you want more of. Hold that word for the rest of the sit. If you'd like, look up one letter of the Gurmukhi alphabet later today and learn its shape. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and notice the letters in it. The bell holds the time.
The learned man of Benares. The pandit who tested Nanak with learning, and, tradition says, heard him sing the Oankar, where every letter points to the One.
screen: `THE LEARNED MAN OF BENARES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: learning bows. Today, take one thing you know well and ask it what it's really about. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: The Oankar, which tradition links to Guru Nanak's meeting with a pandit, is part of the Guru Granth Sahib and is sung and studied by Sikhs, verse by verse through the letters.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Oankar, the One, and the name of the hymn tradition says Nanak sang at Benares.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy man outsmarts a scholar.
what it means: the Guru answers a test of learning with a hymn that turns each letter into a door to the One.
what a scholar hears: the Oankar, in Raag Ramkali, moves through the letters of the alphabet, taking up the pandit's own way of teaching.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi tradition: Nanak and the pandit at Benares

notes: The pandit's name Chatur Das appears in some tellings; confirm. The link between the Oankar and Benares is traditional; the hymn's heading 'Dakhni' ('southern') has led some to place it elsewhere (Onkareshwar). Script says 'tradition says'.
'It opens with Oankar itself, the One, from whom all creation comes, even the gods of creation' paraphrases the opening line (Oankar brahma utpat). Confirm.
Oankar's verses moving through the letters (an acrostic on the paintee) and the wooden slate (patti) detail: confirm.
Ang range 929–938 given from memory; confirm.
Editor: the Oankar's opening paraphrase now names Brahma, as the line does ('Oankar brahma utpat'), instead of 'all creation ... even the gods of creation'.
